# Timeline

Answer field: `model` = `timeline:<topic id>`. Example: "Zeig mir den Zeitstrahl der Weltkriege" gives `timeline:world_wars`.

## Requirements

**Topics.** A closed list of 25 ids in `timeline_topics.h`, generated with the data. The prompt rule and `fetch()` both read that list, so they can't differ. An id not on the list returns false before any URL is built, and Zitro shows the normal Wikipedia picture.

**Data.** Prepared files on the Zitro server, generated by `scripts/make_timeline_data.py` into `webpage2/data/timeline/`:

- `<id>.txt`: UTF-8, tab-separated. Header: `ZTL1`, id, subject QID, title DE, title EN, event count, bundle bytes. One line per event: QID, year, end year or `-`, circa flag, label DE, label EN, image offset, length, width, height, FNV-1a hash, credit or `-`.
- `<id>.jpgs`: all pictures of the timeline, baseline JPEG, one after the other.
- `credits.html`: maker, licence and file link of every picture.

**Dates.** Every date comes from Wikidata, read in this order: P580, P585, P571, P575, P619, P606, P1619, P729, P577 (or the one property named for that event, such as P569 for a person's birth). Deprecated and no-value statements don't count, and preferred rank wins. These get an event rejected:
- no date
- precision coarser than a year (million years for `dinosaurs` and `earth_history`)
- several values with different years
- a year that differs from the person's expectation in the allow-list, which is only a cross-check. It caught the Colosseum (Wikidata 82, usually given as 80), which was then left out

Wikidata's "circa" qualifier (P1480) is shown as "ca.". BC years are negative in Wikidata's JSON; checked with the assassination of Caesar, `-0044`.

**Labels.** Wikidata labels in DE and EN, or `mul`. A short name (P1813) only replaces a label over 30 characters, because short names are often bare abbreviations (WW2, HST). Missing DE or EN falls back to the other language and is logged. Labels with characters outside U+0020-U+05FF are refused.

**Pictures and child safety.** The audience starts at early readers and the topics include war, so no corpses, wounded people, atrocities or gore. How that is enforced:
1. `scripts/make_timeline_allowlist.py` names one exact Commons file per event, chosen by hand. Wikidata's own image is never used automatically: for Pearl Harbor it is an exploding ship, for Caesar's assassination a painting of the killing.
2. Topics marked `sensitive` (world wars, Cold War, Roman Empire, ancient Greece, Middle Ages, Swiss history) accept only the tags portrait, map, vehicle, flag, building, document, nature, artifact.
3. Commons categories are checked against a list of words (corpses, wounded, massacre, execution and so on). This is a second net, not the real check.
4. Every picture was looked at on captioned contact sheets at its prepared size, on 2026-11-06. **The one who looked was the AI that built this, not a person.** A few were enlarged for a closer look; the rest were seen only at that small size, so a small detail could be missed.
5. `scripts/make_timeline_pins.py` pins each looked-at file by SHA-1. A changed Commons file is refused until someone looks again.

What the looking changed: "1944 NormandyLST.jpg" turned out to be soldiers wading ashore from a landing craft, despite its name, and was replaced by a plan drawing of the landing craft. A photo of a young child getting polio drops was removed.

**Decision for a person:** nobody has looked at these pictures except the AI. `make_timeline_data.py --contact-sheets <dir>` writes the sheets, one per topic, so they can be skimmed in a few minutes.

**Deliberately left out.** The world wars timeline doesn't name the Holocaust or the atomic bombings, and shows no Nazi symbols and no portraits of perpetrators. Pearl Harbor shows the memorial, Sarajevo a portrait of the Archduke. The Black Death has no picture. This is a choice about what suits the youngest users, not a statement about history, and it needs a person's decision.

**Fetch.** `<id>.txt` must arrive, within 12 s, or there is no timeline. Then `<id>.jpgs` into PSRAM as a single download, because every extra file would cost another TLS handshake. Total limit 30 s instead of `EDU_LOOKUP_DEADLINE_MS`. Limits: 24 events, 8 KB index, 512 KB bundle. Today's largest bundle is 69 KB.

**A picture is kept only if** all of it arrived, it starts and ends as a JPEG, and its hash matches the index. Otherwise that event has no picture, and the timeline still works. After a stalled download, the pictures that arrived whole are kept. No PSRAM for the bundle: a timeline without pictures.

**Screen.**
- Top line: the time axis. Year marks at one spacing per timeline, gold dots for events.
- Band: picture 240x96 at most. Contained for maps, flags, portraits, documents and artworks, otherwise cropped to fill.
- Year: big, top left, fixed in place, running while the band moves. BC as "v. Chr." / "BC", from a million years as "Mio. Jahre her" / "million years ago". An end year if Wikidata has one.
- Label: up to two lines, broken at spaces and hyphens, under the picture.
- Bottom line: the picture's credit where its licence asks for one, otherwise the timeline's name and "Wikidata". Right side: `3/8`, or "Ende"/"End" on the last event.

**Spacing.** One scale per timeline, set so the median distance between events is 120 px: equal time is equal distance. Limits: 24 px minimum between pictures, 720 px maximum. A time cut to the maximum is marked by a break in the axis, and it can't be read as to scale. A gap of at least 110 px has the time written in it ("21 Jahre").

**Input.**
- Button C: next event. On the last event it goes to the text answer, and the next visit starts at the first event. That is the way out; Button A (new question) also works everywhere.
- Button B: previous event. Stops at the first.
- Tilt: tipping the stick about 20 degrees around the axis through its screen, right side down, moves one event forward; left side down moves back. Going back to level does nothing. Tilt stops at both ends and never leaves the view. Uses `modelGyroDps[2]`, dead zone 15 degrees per second. The direction is the constant `TIMELINE_TILT_SIGN`.

**Performance.** One picture decoded per frame at most, into one of 5 PSRAM sprites (46 KB each) kept for the current event and its neighbours. Pictures are never decoded per frame once in a sprite. Every 5 s the serial log prints `Timeline frame: draw avg .. max .. ms, period avg .. ms, N decodes avg .. max .. ms, ...`. Expect one decode to be visible as a short hitch at the start of a move; this is unmeasured on the stick.

**Not tested on the stick:** everything on the device, including the tilt direction, frame time, decode time, and the fetch against the live server. `model timeline:world_wars` on the serial port tries it.

**Tests.** `tests/timeline/run.sh`: parser with broken and hostile input, picture checks, layout, motion, tilt gesture, year text, label wrap, and every generated file. It also decodes all pictures with `lgfx_tjpgd`, the decoder behind `drawJpg`. Measured here: 164 pictures, average 4.8 KB, largest 11 KB, all decoded without error. Decode time on this computer says nothing about the stick.

## User guide

Ask for a timeline: "Zeig mir den Zeitstrahl der Weltkriege" or "Show me a timeline of space exploration".

Topics: world wars, space exploration, dinosaurs, Roman Empire, inventions, Swiss history, ancient Egypt, ancient Greece, Middle Ages, explorers, aviation, railways, computers, Moon missions, Mars missions, Olympic Games, medicine, scientists, composers, painters, Earth's history, Cold War, famous buildings, communication, cars.

- **Button C:** next event. After the last one you're back at the answer.
- **Button B:** previous event.
- **Tip the stick** to the right for the next event, to the left for the previous one.
- **Button A:** new question.

The big year runs while the band moves. A long way between two pictures means a long time. A small cut in the line at the top means even longer than it looks.

## Release note

- Ask for a timeline and travel through history: tip Zitro or press a button to go from the first satellite to the Moon, with real dates and pictures.

## Sources and licences

- **Wikidata:** dates and labels. CC0, no credit required.
- **Wikimedia Commons:** pictures. Licences used: public domain 84, CC0 5, CC BY 22, CC BY-SA 53. Checked per file from Commons metadata. NC, ND, fair use and GFDL alone are refused. CC BY and CC BY-SA need the maker's name: shown on the bottom line where it fits, and always in `credits.html` with the licence, a link to the file and a note that it was resized and may be cropped. Where Commons' metadata names nobody, the name is copied from the file page into the allow-list (4 files).
- **CC BY-SA means** the resized pictures stay under the same licence.
- `credits.html` must be uploaded with the data, at `https://zitro.spot/data/timeline/credits.html`, and should be linked from the website. Whether a credit file counts as "available" enough is a decision for a person.
